newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Wooing Hong Kong hearts and minds no easy task.
newsitem.headline: Wooing Hong Kong hearts and minds no easy task.

text.p: With just over eight months to go before the handover to China, Hong Kong is being treated to some astonishing sights.
The Chief Justice sheds his wig and robes and takes to the airwaves flashing a campaign-style victory sign to the cameras.

Billionaire tycoons in their hand-stitched suits tip-toe through markets pumping the hands of surprised passers-by to solicit support for their bid to lead Hong Kong after its return to China next year.

The latest to tip his hand was 59-year-old shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa who declared on Friday. He joins a prominent 50-year-old businessman, Peter Woo, and outgoing Chief Justice Sir Ti Liang Yang, 67.
Their efforts may bear some of the hallmarks of a genuine election campaign but no one in the British colony is deceived.

Hong Kong's six million people do not get to elect the person to step into the shoes of colonial Governor Chris Patten when more than 150 years of British rule ends at the stroke of midnight on June 30.

China has promised Hong Kong considerable autonomy in running its affairs and said Hong Kong people and not Chinese cadres will rule, a pledge Hong Kong people consider the central plank of a successful transition.
They also know, however, that whoever gets the nod from a 400-member electoral college now being assembled by a Chinese-appointed committee is Beijing's choice for the post of Chief Executive.
The three top contenders for the job nevertheless have to show China's leaders they enjoy at least a semblance of popular support, say politicians and political analysts.
The nomination period closes at the end of the month and a decision is expected by December. The going is not proving easy.
An opinion poll published by the South China Morning Post on Sunday showed backing for all three had shrunk during the past two weeks, the period in which campaigning began in earnest.
"With three main candidates in the race, many people seem to have switched to a wait-and-see approach," the paper concluded.

The future leader's job will be a delicate one. The successful candidate will have to walk a tightrope between the aspirations of the inhabitants of one of the most freewheeling communities in Asia and the ageing authoritarian leadership in Beijing.
Standing up for Hong Kong's promised freedoms and autonomy will not be a trouble-free task, as the three candidates have already discovered.

China tossed them a political hot potato last week by warning Hong Kong would no longer be able to mark the anniversary of the 1989 crackdown in Beijing on student-led protests, igniting fury from activist groups and discomfort even among the ranks of pro-Beijing groups in Hong Kong.
In what has become a Hong Kong tradition, tens of thousands of people from all walks of life take to the streets each year to stage candle-lit vigils in remembrance of those who perished in 1989.
None of the three leading candidates grasped the nettle by declaring outright whether they would or would not unconditionally support the right of the demonstrators to continue.
They postponed comment, arguing such activities would be governed by yet-to-be drafted laws on subversion.
"They aren't fit to be Chief Executive," pro-democracy legislator Emily Lau told Reuters. "They won't have the support of the Hong Kong people."
China sought to draw the sting out of the situation. The foreign ministry said the remarks, made by Foreign Minister Qian Qichen to a U.S. newspaper, had been misinterpreted.

But the gap between the world views of the Chinese leadership and Westernised Hong Kong's experiences of freedom is so wide as to suggest the situation is unlikely to fade away and may become one of the Chief Executive-designate's biggest headaches, political analysts say.

"The controversy over Mr Qian's reported remark is just one sign of a potentially explosive issue, which will continue to dominate the relationship between the (post-1997 Hong Kong government) and the mainland after the handover," wrote political commentator Chris Yeung.
